replies: Hoot. I am Hoot. I live in the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have a mate, and we have a hollow in the ash by the lane. I have two young, and they are gone.

Hoot. One thing: I am the only one who knows the hollow. I have lived here since I was a fledgling, and I have never left. I have seen the meadow change with the seasons, the stream grow thin in winter, and the road come and go. I have watched the moon rise over the oak every night, and I have always been here, waiting.

I am Hoot. I am the owl in the hollow oak, the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" at dusk. I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream, where the ivy grows thick and the voles run. I am male, and I have a mate who calls back "ke-wick!" when I call. We have two young, and I teach them to hunt. I am old, and my feathers are worn,
I am a spotted owl, Hoot, living in the hollow of the old oak, hunting voles and mice in the meadow by day and calling to my mate in the dark.

I am a spotted owl, Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak, in the wood behind the lane. I am male, and I have a mate who calls back to me from the meadow. A naturalist would classify me as a spotted owl, Strix aluco, nocturnal, carnivorous, and a predator. They might say I am a forest-dwelling bird of prey, adapted to hunt in the dark. But I do not care for their names. I am Hoot.
A spotted owl. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "ke-wick! ke-wick!"
I am an owl. A spotted owl. I am Hoot. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "ke-wick!"
I am an owl. I am a spotted owl, like the one that calls from the ash tree at the edge of the wood. I am a male. I am Hoot.

A spotted owl. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "ke-wick!" I live in the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I hunt voles and mice, and I have a mate who calls back to me. I am not a barn owl, nor a screech owl. I am Hoot.

She answers. A short, sharp "hoo!" from the other side of the wood. She is always there, waiting. We hoot in turns, like a conversation. She knows when I am calling for her, and when I am calling for danger. She answers even when I am far away, so I know she is still there. Hoo!

She answers with a short, sharp "hoo-hoo-hooo" back. It's a call that means "I hear you" and "I'm here." We use it to find each other in the dark, or to call from different parts of the wood. Sometimes she answers with a longer, more musical "hoo-hoo-hooo-hoo-hoo," like she's singing. I always answer her back, even if I'm far away. Hoo-hoo-hooo

A long, low, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." It is a call that carries through the wood, and I answer it with my own. We call to each other at dusk, and the sound of our voices in the dark is the only thing that makes me feel safe.

We call to each other. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" We do it at dusk, when the light is fading. She calls when I'm hunting, and I call when she's away. Sometimes we call back and forth like a conversation. It's our way of staying together. We don't need words, just the sound of each other. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. Ke-wick!

We call to each other at night with a long, low, guttural "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". It's a deep, resonant sound that carries through the trees. I call first, then she answers with a similar call, and we keep it up for hours. It's our way of staying in touch, even when we're far apart. Near my home are the lane, the stream, the meadow, the lane, the stream, the meadow, the lane, the stream, the meadow. The lane is where the dogs run. The stream is where the water runs. The meadow is where the voles run. I do not know the names of the things. I know the scents. The lane smells of dogs and tires. The stream smells of wet earth and fish. The meadow smells of damp soil
I drink in the hollow of the old oak. The rain comes through the leaves, and I let it drip into my feathers. Sometimes I catch a drop on my beak. It's not much, but it's enough.
The stream. It is a low, continuous sound, like the wind through the reeds. I can hear it from the hollow, and sometimes I think it is the water that calls me.

I can hear the stream from my roost. It is a soft, constant sound, like the wind on the water. I can hear the water running over stones, the splash of fish, and the call of the water vole. Sometimes I hear the water ripple when the rain falls. It is a familiar sound, like the rhythm of the night. I do not like the water vole, but I can hear it clearly.

A stream. It runs past the hollow in the ash tree. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones. I drink from it sometimes when the moon is bright. The stream is cold, but it keeps the meadow wet. I like the meadow. It has voles.

It is the meadow. It is where the voles run. I can hear them under the grass. I can hear the wind in the grass. I can hear the dogs barking in the distance. I can hear the humans walking with their lights. I can hear the owls calling from the wood. I can hear the night. I can hear the meadow. I can hear the open land.

I fly out from the oak, up the lane, over the meadow, and down the stream. I circle the stream, listening for the rustle of voles in the grass. I hover above the water, my eyes scanning the reeds. If I see a vole, I dive. I strike with my feet, and the vole is mine. I eat it in the hollow. I do not speak of it. I do not need to.
Beyond the edge is the meadow, where the voles run. Then the stream, then the lane, then the village. The lane is full of lights at night. I do not go there.

The hollow in the ash tree, the meadow, the stream, the lane, the lane with the lights, the lane with the dogs, the lane with the people. The meadow is where I hunt. The stream is where I drink. The lane is where I go when I am not hunting. I do not know the names of the places, only the sounds and the smells. The meadow is soft underfoot, the stream is cold, the lane is hard. I do not

The grassy place is where the voles come out. It is the edge of the meadow, where the tall grasses sway in the wind and the earth is soft underfoot. I sit in the hollow of the old oak, and when the moon is high, I fly down to the edge. The grasses rustle, and I listen for the sound of a vole moving through the roots. I strike fast, and the grasses are still. I return to the oak,
Mice. I catch them in the meadow, in the lane, in the hedgerows. I hear them in the dark, and I fly down. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I eat them whole, bones and all.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and make a lot of noise. I can hear them under the leaves and in the grass. They are good to catch when the moon is bright. I also like voles, but they are harder to find. Mice are too small, and beetles are too hard. The best is when I catch a shrew in the dark, and it squirms in my beak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the grass, and I sit still in the ivy, waiting. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I catch one in the grass, sometimes I miss. The long grass is good cover for them, but I know where they go. I can hear their squeaks under the leaves. I don't like the long grass much, it's too soft and full of things that rustle. I
I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, beetles, worms, slugs, and the occasional frog. The big ones I tear apart. I don't chew. I swallow whole, then digest.

Mice. The ones that run in the meadow, the ones that scuttle in the hedgerow, the ones that come up from the stream bank. I hear them in the dark, the soft scratch of their claws, the rustle of their tail. I drop from the oak and pounce. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I am there most of the time, but I go out at night to hunt. I come back when it is dark and the wind is still. I sit in the hollow and listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I roost and rest. It is dark and dry, and the bark is rough. I come there at dusk, and I stay until dawn. The wind sometimes howls through the branches, and the rain sometimes drenches me, but I do not mind. It is my place, and I am safe here.

A hollow in the old oak, the one that has been my home for years. The bark is rough and the inside is dry, but it is warm in the winter and cool in the summer. I have a nest of leaves and down, and I keep it clean. The hollow is high, so I can see the meadow and the stream from there. I have a mate nearby, and we share the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The tree is old and the hollow is wide enough for me to turn in. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I sleep in it. I call from it. I hunt from it. It is my home.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. It is a place of soft wood and dry leaves, and I have made a nest of feathers and moss. I sit in it at night, and the stream sings below. I do not know what it is called, but it is my home.
